Bank of America Warns Customers Against Sharing Banking Passwords With AI Agents

Bank of America warned customers in an email blast not to share their online banking username and password with any AI assistant or agent acting on their behalf.

The bank said handing over login credentials to an AI tool risks unauthorized account access, fraud-related lockouts, or credential leaks if the assistant itself has a security flaw.

Customers remain fully liable for any activity resulting from credentials they share, under the bank's account agreement.

The notice reflects a wider struggle across banks and payment processors to safely enable AI agents for account access as agentic-commerce tools grow more popular.

Authorities are still offering an $11 million reward for his alleged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk.

⚡️️️️Binance Faces Suspected $2 Billion Crypto Heist

Binance confirmed a security incident and suspended withdrawals on multiple networks after users reported funds draining from its wallets.

Crypto trackers estimate between $2 billion and $5.7 billion was pulled from Binance hot wallets, with Circle and Tether freezing roughly $800 million and $1.56 billion in stablecoins tied to the theft.

No attacker has been identified, and former CEO Changpeng Zhao said he expects affected user funds to be fully covered.

Withdrawals resumed later into the weekend.

Apple Patches Exploited CoreGraphics Zero-Day on Older iPhones

Apple patched a CoreGraphics zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-86950, with iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 updates for older devices released October 26, 2026.

The out-of-bounds write flaw lets a crafted file trigger code execution on devices including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad.

Apple said the flaw may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals running iOS versions before iOS 27.

Capcom Confirms Breach Exposing 11.7 Million Customer Records

Capcom disclosed that unauthorized access to its CAPCOM ID account service exposed 11,774,247 records worldwide.

The exposed data includes email addresses, account creation and login timestamps, login counts, and the IP address used at last login.

Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts without permission, though Capcom says no credit card information was affected.

Capcom has reported the breach to Japanese police and the national privacy regulator as its investigation continues.
